Algebraic-Properties/Identity.title: Identity
Algebraic-Properties/Identity.content:
Overview
Identity is an algebraic property of a set relative to an operation. It states that given a set and a binary operation, there exist an element that leaves every element of the set unchanged when combined with it.
Definition
Given a set \large S and a binary operation \large \circ, there is an element \large e \in S such that for all \large s \in S:
 \large e \circ s = s \space \space and \space \space s \circ e = s
Uniqueness of identity
If an identity element exists for a binary operation on S, then it is unique.

Algebraic-Properties/Invertibility.title: Invertibility
Algebraic-Properties/Invertibility.content:
Overview
Invertibility is an algebraic property of an element relative to a binary operation. It states that an element can be undone by another element under that operation, yielding the identity element.
Let \large (S, \circ) be a set with a binary operation and an identity \large e.
An element \large a \in S is invertible if there exist \large b \in S such that:
\Large  a\circ b = e \space \space and \space \space b \circ a= e 
The element \large b is called an inverse of \large a, and is written as \large a^{-1}.
The property is not the undoing element itself, but the fact that such an undoing element exists.

Algebraic-Structures/Algebraic-Structure.title: Algebraic Structures
Algebraic-Structures/Algebraic-Structure.content:
Overview
Algebraic structures are non-empty sets equipped with operations on such set along with specific axioms these operations must satisfy.
Tags
AlgebraicStructure

Algebraic-Structures/Group.title: Group
Algebraic-Structures/Group.content:
Overview
A group is an algebraic structure consisting of a set equipped and a binary operation that is associative and closed, has an Identity element and for which every element admits an Invertibility.
A group whose binary operation is commutative is called an abelian group.
Tags
AbstractAlgebra AlgebraicStructure

Algebraic-Structures/Magma.title: Magma
Algebraic-Structures/Magma.content:
Overview
A magma is the most basic algebraic structure with a binary operation. It consist of a set and a closed binary operation.
\huge (M, \space *)
A magma with the inclusion of associativity forms a Semigroup.
Tags
AlgebraicStructure

Algebraic-Structures/Monoid.title: Monoid
Algebraic-Structures/Monoid.content:
Overview
A monoid is an algebraic structure consisting of a set equipped with an Identity, along a closed and associative binary operation.
\huge(S, \space *, \space e)
A monoid in which ever element admits an inverse forms a Group.
Tags
AlgebraicStructure AbstractAlgebra

Algebraic-Structures/Semigroup.title: Semigroup
Algebraic-Structures/Semigroup.content:
Overview
A semigroup is an algebraic structure consisting of a set and a closed and associative binary operation.
(S, \space *)
A semigroup with an identity forms a Monoid.
Tags
AbstractAlgebra AlgebraicStructure

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Basis.title: Basis
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Basis.content:
Overview
A basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans the space.
Basis Vector
A basis vector is one of the vectors in a chosen set that forms a basis. As a result, every vector in the space can be written uniquely as a Linear Combination of these vectors.
The number of basis vectors equals the dimension of the space, and whether a vector is a “basis vector” depends entirely on the chosen basis—there is nothing intrinsic about a specific vector being a basis vector outside that context.
Tags
VectorSpace

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Column.title: Column Space
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Column.content:
Overview
The column space of a linear equation matrix is the space of possible outputs/solutions to the system of equations for that matrix.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Determ.title: Determinant
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Determ.content:
Overview
The determinant is a property of a linear operator, defined as the factor by which area, volume or n-volume are scaled, and indicates whether the transformation preserves or reverses orientation.
Compute the determinant
2-dimensional space
To compute the determinant of a linear operator on a 2-dimensional vector space, we represent it in a basis as a 2 \times 2 matrix T, and define det(T) = ad - bc.
\large T = \begin{bmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d 
\end{bmatrix}, \space \space \space \det(T) = ad - bc
3-dimensional space
For a linear operator on a 3-dimensional vector space, its matrix representation is a 3 \times 3 matrix:
\large T = \begin{bmatrix}
a & b & c \\
d & e & f \\ 
g & h & i \\
\end{bmatrix}
The determinant is:
\large \det(T) = a(ei-fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg)
VectorSpace

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Dual-S.title: Dual Space
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Dual-S.content:
Overview
A dual space V^* of a Vector Space V over a field k is the set of all linear functionals from V to k.
\huge V^* = \{f: V \to k \space | \space is \space linear\} 
V^* is itself a vector space with respect to the natural pointwise operations.
Tags
VectorSpace

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Eigenv.title: Eigenvector
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Eigenv.content:
LinearAlgebra
An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose direction is preserved by a Linear Transformation.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.title: Linear Combination
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.content:
Overview
A linear combination \large V is a sum of scalar multiples of vectors defined as \large V = av + bw where \large a, b are scalars and \large v, w are vectors.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.title: Linear Form
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.content:
Overview
A linear form also called linear functional, is a special type of Linear Transformation that takes a vector from a Vector Space \large V and returns a single scalar from the ground field \large k, preserving the vector space operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication.
\huge T:V \to k  
Tags
VectorSpace

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.title: Linear Transformation
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Linear.content:
Overview
A linear transformation is a function that takes a vector as input and produces another vector in the same or a different vector space.
\huge T: V \mapsto W 
It is defined purely by how it maps vectors, not by distances or geometric shapes.
A linear transformation may stretch, rotate, reflect or shear space, but it must preserve vector addition and scalar multiplication.
Straight lines through the origin remain straight and the origin stays fixed.
Classification
Linear Operator
A linear operator is defined as a linear transformation from a vector space to itself.
Linear Map
A linear map can be used to indicate that the linear transformation is from a vector space to another.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Null-S.title: Null Space
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Null-S.content:
Overview
The null space of a linear transformation from one vector space to another, is the subset of the first vector space consisting of all vectors that the transformation maps to zero in the codomain.

\Large null(T) = \{\space v \in V \space |\space T(v) = 0_W\space \}

The null space captures what gets collapsed to nothing by the transformation.
If a vector lies in the null space, applying \large T produces no effect. The transformation cannot distinguish that vector from the zero vector.
The null space lives entirely in the domain \large V, not the codomain \large W.
The null space is always a subspace of \large V. This makes the null space a geometric and algebraic object that measures how much information the transformation lose.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Ring/P.title: Polynomial
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Ring/P.content:
Overview
A polynomial is an algebraic object defined as the finite sum of powers of a variable multiplied by coefficients, for which there is only one coefficient per power such that (a_0 + a_1X + a_2X^2 + ... + a_nX^n)

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Ring/R.title: Ring
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Ring/R.content:
AlgebraicStructure
A ring is a type of algebraic structure. It consist of a set with two operations

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Span.title: Span
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Span.content:
Overview
A set spans a vector space if every vector in the space can be written as a Linear Combination of the vectors in the set.
Tags
VectorSpace

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Subspa.title: Subspace
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Subspa.content:
Overview
A subspace of a vector space V is a non-empty subset (W \subseteq V) that is also closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Vector.title: Vector Space
Algebraic-Structures/Vector-Space/Vector.content:
Overview
A vector space is an algebraic structure defined as a set \large V together with two operations called vector addition (which combines two vectors) and scalar multiplication (which scales a vector by a scalar).
A vector space is always defined over a field of scalars.
Vector
A vectors is simply an element of a vector space (\large v∈V).
There is nothing intrinsically “vector-like” about an object by itself.
Anything that participates correctly in vector addition and scalar multiplication qualifies as a vector.
Vector Addition
Vector addition takes two vectors and returns another one.
\Large +: V \times V \to V
Vector addition must satisfy the following properties:


Closure: adding two vectors produces another vector inside the same space.
\large \forall u,v \in V, \space u + v \in V


Commutativity: the order of addition does not alter the result.
\large \forall u,v \in V, \space u + v = v + u.


Associativity: grouping of addition does not matter.
\large \forall u,v,w \in V, \space (u + v) + w = u + (v + w).


Invertible: every vector has an additive inverse.
\large v+(-v) = (-v)+v=0.


Identity: there is a vector that changes nothing when added (think adding zero).
\large \forall v \in V, \space v + 0 = 0 + v = v.


Scalar Multiplication
Scalar multiplication scales a vector by a scalar.
\Large \cdot: F \times V \to V
Scalar multiplication must satisfy the following properties:

Associativity: scaling by one scalar and then another is the same as scaling by their product.
\large \forall a,b \in F, \forall v \in V, \space\space (ab) \cdot v = a \cdot (b \cdot v).
Identity: multiplying a vector by the scalar one leaves it unchanged (think multiplying by 1).
\large \forall v \in V = 1 \cdot v = v.
Distributivity: over vector addition and over scalar addition.
\large \forall a \in F, \forall u,v \in V, \space\space a \cdot (u +v) = a \cdot u + a \cdot v.
\large \forall a, b \in F, \forall v \in V, \space\space (a +b) \cdot v = a \cdot v + b \cdot v.

Decimal-(Base-10).title: Decimal (Base 10)
Decimal-(Base-10).content:
Overview
Decimals are a numeric system based on powers of 10. It has 10 characters to represent quantities (0-9). It’s the most common used numeric system by humans.
Operations
Steps to add decimals
Steps to subtract decimals
Steps to multiply
Steps to divide decimals with fractional parts

Turn the divisor into a whole number:
If the divisor has decimals, multiply both the divisor and the dividend by 10^n, where n is the number of decimal places in the divisor, to make the divisor a whole number.



                  
                  EXAMPLE
                  
                

Problem: 18\div0.6
The divisor (0.6) has 1 decimal place. Multiply both the divisor and the dividend by 10 to make the divisor a whole number:
18 \div 0.6 = \frac{0.6×10}{18×10}​= \frac{180}{6}




Perform the Division:
Divide the numbers as if they were whole numbers.


Adjust the Decimal Point in the Result:
The position of the decimal in the dividend determines the placement of the decimal in the result.

Glossary.title: Glossary
Glossary.content:
Relationship:
A general, unconstrained connection or link between elements of two sets.
Mapping:
A precise, rule-based assignment of the elements from one set to another. One-to-one and deterministic.
Synonym with: Function, Transformation.
Association:
Any pairing between of elements of two sets.
Sum:
The result from addition.
Difference:
The result from a subtraction.
Term:
Multiple:
A multiple is the result of multiplying any integer by another.
Product:
The result from a multiplication.
Factor:
A factor is any integer that divides another integer without leaving a remainder.
Quotient:
The whole number result from a division.
Remainder:
The amount left over after division when one number does not divide another exactly.

Number.title: Number
Number.content:
Overview
Numbers are mathematical objects used as a representation of quantity, position or value.
Number Sets
Natural Numbers
These are the fundamental set of numbers, typically starting at 1 and continuing indefinitely. These numbers are mostly used for counting objects.
\huge \{1,2,3,…\}
Integers
Extend natural numbers by including their negative counterpart and 0. These numbers are used to express quantities with deficits (e.g., accounting, temperature).
\{ \huge …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …\}
Rational Numbers
Rational numbers \huge\mathbb{Q} are any number that can be written as a [fraction] where the numerator and denominator are integers.  Rational numbers include terminating and repeating Decimal (Base 10).
Irrational Numbers
Real Numbers
Real numbers form the complete set of all numbers that can be placed on a one dimensional number line. This set includes all rational and all irrational numbers.
Tags
SetTheory NumberTheory

Sets/Function.title: Function
Sets/Function.content:
A function is a relationship between two sets called domain (source set) and codomain (target set) where a well-defined rule, assigns exactly one element (output) in the codomain to each element (input) in the domain.
\huge f: A \rightarrow B ~~or~~ f: A \rightarrow A
A function is often denoted by a letter such as f, g or h.
\Huge f(x)=x+a, ~ and ~ if ~ a=2,~then ~ f(2)=2+2=4

Sets/Operation.title: Operation
Sets/Operation.content:
An operation is a Function from a set to itself (f: A \rightarrow A)
Binary Operations

Sets/Set-Operations.title: Set Operations
Sets/Set-Operations.content:
Cartesian Product
The cartesian product is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b) from a set A and a set B.
\huge A \times B = \{(a,b)~|~a \in A \wedge b \in B\}
Power Set
A power set is the set of all subsets of a set.

Sets/Set-Properties.title: Set Properties
Sets/Set-Properties.content:
Cardinality
The number of elements in a set a.k.a. its size, is called cardinality. It is noted using the set letter (\large A) between two pipes (\large |A|).
Lets say that \large A=\{a,b,c,d,e,f \} thus \large |A| = 5
Counting
Counting is the process of determining the cardinality of a set. Counting corresponds to assigning a natural number to represent the number of distinct elements.
We can define a counting function as:
 \Large f(X) = |X|
Countable Sets
A set is countable if its elements can be put into a bijection with the natural numbers \large \mathbb{N}. This includes all finite sets (\large\{1,2,3\}) and some infinite sets, like \large \mathbb{N} itself, \large \mathbb{Z}, and \large \mathbb{Q}.
Uncountable Sets
A set is uncountable if no such correspondence with \large \mathbb{N} exists. For example the set of real numbers \large \mathbb{R} is uncountable, as shown by Cantor’s diagonal argument. This proves that \large \mathbb{R} has a strictly larger cardinality than \large \mathbb{N}.
Tags
SetTheory

Sets/Set-Theory.title: Set Theory
Sets/Set-Theory.content:
Lousily defined, a set is a collection of objects that are referred to as elements.
Sets
A set (S) is any collection of definite, distinguishable objects of our intuition or of our intellect to be conceived as a whole.
The objects are called elements or members. Membership is a relation between objects and sets.
A set its regarded as a single entity.
Principles
Extension

Two sets are equal if (and only if) they have the same members.

The equality of two sets X and Y will be noted as X=Y and the inequality as X \not = B.
Abstraction

Every property determines a set.

\{ x|P(x) \}: The set of all x such that property P(x) holds.
References
Stoll, R. (1963). Set theory and logic. Dover Publications.
Loose ideas to consider
G. Cantor
Transcendental numbers
Function, Equivalence relation and ordering relation
Cantorian = Naive

index.title: Welcome to Fermath
index.content:
My name is Sebastian Ferreira, and this is my math archive.
On 2024 I decided to reteach myself all the math I didn’t properly pay attention to since school, with the goal to genuinely understand it and being able to teach it.
This wiki is intended as a digital garden. Notes will evolve over time as my understanding and explanations improve.
Rather than a linear course, the content is organized into atomic entries. The idea is to let you learn what you need without forcing you to repeat what you already know.
Academic mathematics is often formal and highly abstract, which creates a steep learning curve for beginners. That abstraction is necessary, since mathematics is ultimately a language for abstraction.
I understand the need of mathematicians to keep math abstract, after all, is a language for abstraction.
Still, I aim to provide a bridge between everyday intuitions and the formal definitions.
This wiki is not meant to replace primary learning materials. Use it as a support when you feel stuck or when a definition feels opaque.
The focus here is pedagogical rather than fully rigorous. Examples are meant as stepping stones. The underlying mathematics usually goes further than what is shown.
Ultimately, to truly learn mathematics, you have to do it yourself.
See the Vector Space for how to get started.
